newsitem.title: CHILE: "Stray Dog" carries reed raft crew to Easter Island.
newsitem.headline: "Stray Dog" carries reed raft crew to Easter Island.

text.p: The multinational crew of a failed Spanish-led expedition aiming to promote universal brotherhood by sailing around the world in a primitive reed raft landed safely in Easter Island on Monday on board the U.S. yacht "Stray Dog," island authorities said.
"They arrived in good spirits and good health," a spokeswoman for the Chilean-administered island in the middle of the Pacific Ocean told Reuters by telephone.
She said the 11-member crew and two stowaways rescued on Sunday two days after their vessel was torn in two by a storm said they did not want to undergo medical examinations.
The 99-foot-long (30-metre) Mata Rangi (Eyes of Paradise) set sail from Easter Island three weeks ago using only primitive methods for its voyage around around the world.
The ship, built by Bolivian Indians and Easter Islanders, was modelled after ancient Inca boats in an attempt to show ancient cultures could cross oceans.

But the Mata Rangi's woes began even before it was smashed by rough weather, leaving the crew drifting about on a ragtag raft strung together out of wreckage. Two Easter Island stowaways with criminal records were found hidden among provisions a few days out at sea.

The expedition was backed by UNESCO as a mission to promote peace and tolerance. The Spanish royal family also supported it, although Spain's Prince Felipe was unable to officially launch the expedition as planned due to bad weather and last-minute technical hitches.
The private U.S.-flagged Stray Dog was in Easter Island when the Mata Rangi's SOS signal went out and left immediately on the rescue mission with a Chilean maritime official on board.
Spaniard Kitin Munoz led the Mata Rangi expedition with an official crew of eight Polynesians and two Bolivian Indians. Jose Munoz said in Madrid on Sunday he was sure his brother would try again.
